title: ConfigMaps and Secrets
intro: Apps need configuration and credentials without baking them into the image. ConfigMaps handle plain config, Secrets handle sensitive values.

steps.prompt: Create a ConfigMap named 'app-config' with a key APP_MODE set to 'production'.
steps.explanation: ConfigMaps store non-sensitive config as key-value pairs, which pods can mount as env vars or files.
steps.why: For more than a couple of keys you'd reach for '--from-file=' or '--from-env-file=' instead of stacking multiple '--from-literal' flags — literal is best for one or two quick values like this single key.

steps.fake_output:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: app-config
data:
  APP_MODE: production
steps.explanation: Plain text, fully visible — this is why secrets exist separately for sensitive values.
steps.why: 'kubectl describe configmap app-config' also works and is easier to skim, but -o yaml shows the exact structure you'd need if you were about to copy this into a manifest.

steps.prompt: Create a Secret named 'db-creds' with a key DB_PASSWORD set to 'hunter2'.
steps.explanation: Secrets are base64-encoded (not encrypted by default!) and access-controlled separately via RBAC.
steps.why: 'generic' is the type here because this is an arbitrary key-value secret. Kubernetes also has purpose-built types like 'docker-registry' (for image pull credentials) and 'tls' (for cert/key pairs) — use those instead when they fit.

steps.fake_output:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: db-creds
data:
  DB_PASSWORD: aHVudGVyMg==
steps.explanation: That's just base64, not encryption — anyone who can read Secrets in this namespace can decode it instantly. Real security comes from RBAC and, ideally, an external secrets manager.
steps.why: This is deliberately showing the risky habit: 'kubectl describe secret' hides the value by default, but -o yaml still prints it (base64-encoded, trivially reversible) — which is exactly why Secrets alone aren't real security.
